items.q: (A) No sooner the bell had rung than (B) the whole class rushed out (C) into the corridor, (D) leaving their books scattered across the desks.
options: No sooner the bell had rung
items.correction: No sooner had the bell rung
items.explanation: After the negative adverbial No sooner the auxiliary and subject invert: No sooner had the bell rung than…

items.q: (A) The head coach demanded that every player (B) attends the extra practice session (C) on Saturday, (D) regardless of how tired they felt.
items.explanation: Verbs of demanding (demand, insist, suggest) take a that-clause in the subjunctive, so the base form attend is needed, not attends.

items.q: (A) Walking along the cliff path (B) at dawn, (C) the lighthouse came into view (D) far sooner than we had expected.
items.explanation: A dangling modifier: the participle clause Walking along the cliff path must describe the subject of the main clause, and a lighthouse cannot walk.

items.q: (A) If the council had repaired the bridge (B) last spring, (C) the villagers (D) would not have driven twenty extra kilometres to town at this very moment.
items.explanation: A mixed conditional: a past condition (had repaired) with a present result (at this very moment) takes would be driving, not the past-result form would have driven.

items.q: (A) The scientists did a discovery (B) that could (C) fundamentally alter (D) our understanding of how coral reefs recover after bleaching.
items.explanation: The verb that collocates with discovery is make: you make a discovery, never do one.

items.q: Her essay argues that the city should (A) invest in cycle lanes, (B) restricting parking in the centre (C) and (D) make public transport free for students.
items.explanation: Parallelism: the three actions after should must share the same form (invest…, restrict…, and make…), so the -ing form breaks the series.

items.q: (A) I wish (B) my grandmother (C) is still alive to see (D) how much the orchard she planted has grown.
items.explanation: A wish about a present situation that is not true takes the past subjunctive: I wish she were/was still alive, not is.

items.q: (A) It was (B) not until the final whistle (C) that the exhausted defenders (D) realise how close they had come to losing.
items.explanation: In the cleft It was not until… that… the whole sentence is set in the past, so the verb in the that-clause must be past too: realised.

items.q: (A) A large amount of volunteers (B) turned up (C) to clear the riverbank, (D) far more than the organisers had catered for.
items.explanation: Amount of goes with uncountable nouns; countable plural volunteers needs a large number of.

items.q: It was (A) such (B) a dreadful weather (C) on the day of the picnic that (D) hardly anyone bothered to leave the house.
options: on the day of the picnic
items.explanation: Weather is uncountable and never takes a: such dreadful weather that….

items.q: (A) Hardly had (B) the pilot announced the descent (C) than the plane (D) hit a pocket of turbulence over the mountains.
items.explanation: Hardly/Scarcely… when is the fixed pair; than belongs only with No sooner.

items.q: (A) The expedition pressed on (B) towards the summit (C) for another six hours (D) despite the visibility was almost zero.
items.explanation: Despite is a preposition and cannot introduce a clause with a finite verb; use the conjunction although (or despite the visibility being).

items.q: (A) Seldom I have seen (B) such a fiercely contested final, (C) with the lead changing hands (D) four times in the last ten minutes.
items.explanation: A fronted negative adverb such as Seldom triggers subject–auxiliary inversion: Seldom have I seen.

items.q: (A) Not until the last guest left (B) the hosts realised (C) that the birthday cake (D) had never been taken out of the fridge.
options: Not until the last guest left
items.explanation: When Not until… opens the sentence, the main clause inverts: Not until the last guest left did the hosts realise.

items.q: (A) Whereas most reptiles lay eggs, (B) some species of snake (C) giving birth (D) to live young in cooler climates.
items.explanation: The main clause after the Whereas clause has no finite verb; the participle giving must become the present simple give.

items.q: (A) Exhausted but happy, (B) the climbers (C) reached base camp (D) short before the storm broke over the ridge.
items.explanation: An adverb is needed to modify the conjunction phrase before the storm broke: shortly before, not the adjective short.

items.q: (A) Being lived abroad for a decade, (B) my aunt (C) finds the winters here (D) far harsher than she remembers.
options: Being lived abroad for a decade
items.correction: Having lived abroad for a decade
items.explanation: An earlier, completed action is expressed with a perfect participle (Having lived); Being lived is a passive form and live is not used passively here.

items.q: (A) It is the lack of funding, not of talent, (B) what holds back (C) many of the region's (D) most promising young athletes.
options: It is the lack of funding
items.explanation: A cleft sentence (It is X that…) is completed by that, never by what.

items.q: (A) Rarely does (B) a debut novel (C) receives such unanimous acclaim (D) from critics who normally agree on nothing.
items.explanation: Once the auxiliary does carries the tense in the inverted structure, the main verb reverts to its base form: Rarely does a debut novel receive.

items.q: (A) Not once (B) during the entire trek (C) did the guide (D) lost his patience with the slowest members of the group.
items.explanation: In the inverted structure the auxiliary did already marks the past, so the main verb stays in the base form: did the guide lose.

items.q: (A) It were the quiet villages of the interior, rather than the beaches, (B) that left (C) the deepest impression on the travellers (D) during their month in Portugal.
options: It were the quiet villages of the interior
items.correction: It was the quiet villages of the interior
items.explanation: In a cleft sentence the dummy subject It is always singular, so the verb is was even when the focused noun is plural.

items.q: (A) Scarcely had the orchestra (B) begin the overture (C) when the lights (D) flickered and died across the entire hall.
items.explanation: Scarcely had… is the past perfect, so it needs the past participle begun, not the base form begin.

items.q: (A) The lecture was (B) so densely packed with data (C) as few students (D) managed to take any useful notes.
items.explanation: The result structure is so + adjective + that; as cannot introduce the result clause.

items.q: (A) I wish (B) the neighbours (C) would stop (D) to play the drums after midnight when everyone else is trying to sleep.
items.explanation: Stop + -ing means to cease an activity; stop + to-infinitive means to pause in order to do something, which makes no sense here.

items.q: (A) The fewer time you spend scrolling before bed, (B) the more easily (C) you will fall asleep, (D) or so the sleep researchers claim.
items.explanation: Time here is uncountable, so its comparative quantifier is less; fewer is reserved for countable plurals.

items.q: (A) The teacher suggested (B) us to keep a vocabulary notebook (C) rather than (D) relying on translation apps for every unfamiliar word.
items.explanation: Suggest is never followed by object + to-infinitive; it takes a that-clause (suggested that we keep) or an -ing form (suggested keeping).

items.q: (A) If the glacier (B) were still the size it was in 1950, (C) the valley would have had (D) a reliable water supply throughout every summer.
options: were still the size it was in 1950
items.explanation: A present unreal condition (were still) pairs with a present result (would have); would have had points to a past result that the sentence does not describe.

items.q: (A) The lifeguard asked (B) the boys (C) whether they had seen the warning flag (D) and did they understand what it meant.
options: whether they had seen the warning flag
items.explanation: A reported yes/no question keeps statement word order and is introduced by whether/if: and whether they understood, not the direct form did they understand.

items.q: (A) The committee insisted that the report is submitted (B) by Friday, (C) a deadline (D) which several members considered unrealistic.
options: The committee insisted that the report is submitted
items.correction: The committee insisted that the report be submitted
items.explanation: After insist that expressing a demand, the that-clause takes the subjunctive base form: the report be submitted.

items.q: (A) If only (B) the referee has checked (C) the replay, (D) the goal would have been ruled out and the match saved.
items.explanation: A regret about the past after If only takes the past perfect (had checked), matching the past result would have been ruled out.

items.q: (A) After months of negotiation, (B) the two clubs (C) finally reached to an agreement (D) over the transfer fee for the young striker.
items.explanation: Reach is a transitive verb that takes its object directly: reach an agreement, with no to.

items.q: (A) Of all the paintings in the exhibition, (B) the small portrait by the doorway (C) attracted (D) the most attention than any other.
items.explanation: Than demands a comparative: more attention than any other; the superlative the most cannot be followed by than.

items.q: (A) If I would have known (B) how steep the trail was, (C) I would be sitting in a café now (D) instead of nursing two blistered feet.
options: I would be sitting in a café
items.explanation: The if-clause of a past unreal condition takes the past perfect (If I had known); would never appears in that clause.

items.q: (A) The documents (B) referred in the article (C) were finally released (D) after a decade of legal wrangling.
items.explanation: The phrasal verb is refer to, and the particle stays in the reduced passive participle clause: the documents referred to in the article.

items.q: (A) The manager, (B) together with two assistants, (C) were interviewing candidates (D) all afternoon in the small office behind the shop.
items.explanation: A phrase introduced by together with does not change the number of the subject; the manager is singular, so the verb is was.

items.q: (A) Being a keen photographer, (B) my uncle (C) is always on the lookout (D) of unusual cloud formations whenever he drives across the plains.
items.explanation: The fixed expression is on the lookout for something; of is not possible after lookout.

items.q: (A) Much of the equipments (B) the expedition relied on (C) had been donated (D) by a local climbing club the previous winter.
items.explanation: Equipment is uncountable and has no plural; much of the equipment is the only possible form.

items.q: (A) The documentary (B) has attracted widely praise (C) for its unflinching portrayal (D) of life in the mining towns of the north.
items.explanation: A noun (praise) is modified by an adjective, so the adverb widely must become widespread; attract widespread praise is the collocation.

items.q: (A) What the coach (B) values most (C) are the players' willingness (D) to learn from defeat, not their raw speed.
items.explanation: A nominal what-clause used as subject is singular, and the complement willingness is singular too, so the verb must be is.

items.q: (A) The village where my father grew up (B) has changed so much (C) that he no longer recognises (D) the street which he was born.
options: The village where my father grew up
the street which he was born
items.correction: the street where he was born
items.explanation: Which would need to be the object of a verb or preposition; a place in which something happened takes the relative adverb where (or in which).
